title: Dattatreya's last teacher: the wasp
hookLine: a wandering sage's last teacher is a wasp, and under Patanjali's strangest powers runs the same rule: you become what you dwell on
carry: you become what you dwell on
tomorrow: Dhruva, the boy who became the pole star
last: THE HANDFUL OF RICE — A MOOD, NOT ITS REASON.

lines: THE GRUB BECOMES WHAT IT HOLDS.
cards: On day four hundred thirty-nine you met Dattatreya, the wandering sage who named twenty-four teachers, among them an arrow-maker who never looked up. The last teacher on his list is the strangest.
A wasp, the Bhagavata says, carries a small grub into its mud nest and shuts it in. The grub, trapped, thinks of nothing but the wasp, out of sheer fear.
And in the old telling, it thinks so hard that it becomes a wasp itself. Old India believed that about the potter wasp. The lesson was never really about bugs.

teach.h: LOVE, HATRED, FEAR: THE MIND TAKES ITS FORM.
teach.b: Whatever a person fixes the whole mind on, out of love, hatred or fear, that person comes to take its form. It's one of Hinduism's big ideas: you become what you dwell on. You've met it before.
On day one eighty-seven, King Bharata's last thought was a deer. On day four forty-two, Narada said even Kamsa reached Krishna, by fear. Now Patanjali builds powers on the same rule.
Sutra 3.21: by samyama on the body's form, the yogi can't be seen. Antardhana, disappearing. Sutra 3.23: by samyama on friendliness and the others, their strengths.
Those are the four attitudes from book one: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity. Sutra 3.24: by samyama on strengths, the strength of an elephant.
The classical commentators take these as real powers, and some in the tradition still do.
Some modern teachers read them as pictures of the wasp's rule: hold friendliness completely, and you grow friendly; hold strength, and you grow strong.
And invisibility? One reading: the ego that no longer needs to be noticed.

teach.h: JAPA: THE RULE, USED ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: This is why Hindus keep a name of God going under the breath, japa, and set a form of God before the eyes in puja. Not to impress anyone. To grow like what they love.

teach.h: YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DWELL ON.
teach.b: So it's worth asking, honestly, what you dwell on most. The feed you scroll last thing at night is a kind of wasp too.

how: Hindus practice japa, repeating a name of God, and keep a chosen form of God before the eyes in puja, trusting the old teaching that the mind takes the form of what it dwells on; in the Yoga tradition, the classical commentators treat the siddhis as real attainments, while some modern teachers read them symbolically.

o: a spirit's form that no one can see
antardhana: the power of not being seen
hiding your true feelings from others

games.q: the wasp's rule — tap the pairs.

games.q: your family keeps a picture of Krishna in the kitchen, and your nani says his name all day. by Dattatreya's wasp, what's the point?
o: to grow like what you love, by dwelling on it.
to show visitors the family is religious.
to keep bad luck out of the kitchen.
games.why: the wasp's lesson in the Bhagavata: whatever the mind holds completely, it takes the form of. japa and a form of God in view are that rule, used on purpose.

practice: Choose one name to dwell on: Ram, Krishna, Om namah Shivaya, whatever your family says. Repeat it softly or silently with the breath.
If you don't pray, rest on friendliness instead, the warmth you'd feel greeting an old friend at the door. When the mind wanders, come back to the name, or the warmth. You're becoming what you hold.

wordCard.voice: Invisibility. Antardhana in Sanskrit, the first power in today's sutras. One reading: what disappears is the need to be seen.

orig.note: Sanskrit antardhāna: disappearance, vanishing from sight; the power of 3.21.

carryVoice: Your line: you become what you dwell on. Dattatreya learned it from a wasp. That's day four seventy.
